title: FRM Quant, Lesson 3: Machine learning in risk management - and its three traps
subtitle: Overfitting, data leakage, and a model that is accurate but that nobody can explain
whyItMatters: Machine learning has arrived in credit scoring, fraud detection and trade surveillance. It also brings failure modes quite unlike those of traditional statistical models, and the old model risk management framework does not catch them automatically.
openingQuestion: A credit scoring model reaches 99% accuracy on the training data and 71% on new data. What is the clearest problem?
openingOptions: The new data is of lower quality than the training data
The model is overfitted and has learned the noise as well
The model needs more explanatory variables to raise its accuracy
The classification threshold is set wrongly, so the error rate rises
explanation: A large gap between in-sample and out-of-sample results is the classic signature of overfitting: the model is flexible enough to memorise random features that exist only in the training set. Adding variables makes it worse, not better. The fix runs the other way - reduce complexity, add a regularisation penalty, and above all use cross-validation to select the model rather than the in-sample result.

diagram.label: Split the data: training, validation, and a test set never touched
Select the model on the validation set, never on the test set
For time series: split by time, never at random
Being able to explain the output is a requirement, not a nice-to-have

realWorldExample.description: A common form of data leakage: feeding in a variable that only exists once a transaction has already been flagged as suspicious - the processing status, say, or a note from the investigations team. The model reaches near-perfect accuracy in testing and is useless in production, because at the moment a prediction is needed those variables do not exist yet.

quiz.question: Why must time series data not be split randomly into training and test sets?
options: Because time series data is always non-normally distributed
Because a random split makes the training set smaller than needed
Because the model gets to see the future when predicting the past
Because observations in a time series carry different weights
quiz.explanation: A random split puts December's observations in the training set and June's in the test set, so the model learns from the future in order to predict the past. The test result comes out artificially attractive and collapses the moment the model goes live, where the future does not exist yet. The other answers point at properties that are either untrue or beside the point: a random split does not change the size of either set, weighting is a modelling choice rather than a splitting rule, and non-normality would be a problem for the estimator, not for the split.

quiz.question: What does data leakage mean in model building?
options: The model was trained on data belonging to a different institution
Customer data escaped to the outside world during the training run
The training set contains many missing values that were never handled
Information available only after the prediction date got into the inputs
quiz.explanation: The leakage here is a leakage in time, not in security. It produces an outstanding test result that then disappears completely on deployment - and because the initial result was so attractive, it tends to be found late. Confidentiality breaches and unhandled missing values are real problems with real fixes, but neither of them inflates a backtest, and training on another institution's data is a representativeness question rather than a leak. The test that catches leakage is walking through every input and asking whether it existed on the prediction date.

quiz.question: Why is explainability a hard requirement for a credit model?
options: Because the firm has to state a reason for every loan it declines
Because an explainable model always achieves higher accuracy anyway
Because complex models consume far too much computing resource
Because credit data has few variables, so no complex model is needed
quiz.explanation: In many jurisdictions an applicant who is refused credit has the right to know why, and the supervisor needs to check that the model does not discriminate. The answer that the model decided so is not legally sufficient - accuracy does not substitute for the duty to explain. The claim that explainable models are also more accurate is false, and stating it that way misses the point: the trade-off is real, and it is resolved by law rather than by performance. Compute cost is an engineering concern that no regulator weighs here.

quiz.question: What problem does cross-validation solve?
options: It raises the accuracy the model achieves on the training set
It picks the complexity without ever touching the test set
It removes the need for a separate held-out test set entirely
It handles the missing values present in the raw input dataset
quiz.explanation: If you use the test set to select parameters and then report results on that same set, the final number has already been made optimistic. Cross-validation creates splits inside the training set to compare models, keeping the test set clean for a single evaluation at the end. That is exactly why it does not remove the need for a held-out set - it protects one. It does nothing for missing values, which are handled in preprocessing, and it does not raise training accuracy; if anything it exposes how much of that accuracy was memorisation.

quiz.question: Why does a machine learning model need more continuous monitoring after deployment than a traditional one?
options: Because it cannot recompute its output when the inputs change
Because its source code is more prone to engineering bugs
Because the relationships it learned can drift as market behaviour changes
Because the regulator demands a monthly report for this class of model alone
quiz.explanation: A machine learning model captures complex relationships in past data without needing an economic hypothesis behind them. When behaviour changes, a model with a theoretical structure degrades gradually, while a purely data-driven one can break abruptly with nobody seeing it coming. That is a property of what was learned, not of the code or the reporting calendar: these models recompute on new inputs perfectly well, and no supervisor imposes a separate monthly cycle on them.

practicePrompt.question: A default prediction model reaches an AUC of 0.94 on the test set, but the test set was split AT RANDOM from five years of data. What does 0.94 tell you?
options: Nothing yet: the model saw the future while it was learning
The model discriminates very well and is ready to go live
More inputs are needed to push the AUC above the 0.95 mark
The model is overfitting, so the variable count must come down
practicePrompt.explanation: A random split means a loan from March 2021 can sit in the test set while a loan from September 2023 sits in the training set. The model learns on the future and is then scored on the past, and the economic conditions of the later period leak into the parameters. An AUC of 0.94 therefore measures a problem that does not exist in production, where today you only have data up to today. The right split is by time: train up to a cut-off, test after it. Nor is the problem overfitting in the ordinary sense - cutting the variable count does not repair a wrong split.

keyTakeaways: A large gap between in-sample and out-of-sample results signals overfitting - adding variables makes it worse
Time series data must be split by time; a random split lets the model see the future
Data leakage is leakage in time: a variable that only exists after the prediction date gets into the inputs
Explainability is a legal obligation for a credit model, not a feature to be traded away for accuracy

summary.keyIdea: Machine learning trades economic assumptions for raw fitting power. That trade is acceptable, provided the validation framework is tight enough to catch failure modes traditional models never had.

application.message: When you assess a machine learning model, ask two questions before any others: how was the data split, and does every input variable exist at the moment the prediction has to be made.

sections.text: A model that reaches 99% on training data is not good news. With financial data it is almost always bad news.

A model flexible enough will fit everything in the training set, including random features that never repeat. That is why the gap between in-sample and out-of-sample results is a more trustworthy measure than accuracy itself - and why the fix is to reduce complexity rather than to add variables.
Time leakage, the hardest trap to see

If an input variable only exists once the outcome is known, the model is reading the answer. The test results are therefore outstanding, and it is precisely that excellence which stops anyone from being suspicious. The only reliable check is to walk through every variable and ask whether it exists at the moment the prediction is needed.

For a credit decision, the firm has to be able to say why it refused, and the supervisor has to be able to check whether the model discriminates. In that setting, a model that is a few percent more accurate but cannot be explained is usually a model that cannot be used - and this trade-off is not a technical choice.

sections.label: Worth remembering
sections.text: A model with economic theory behind it degrades gradually as the market changes. A purely data-driven model can break abruptly - so it needs tighter monitoring, not looser.
Time leakage, illustrated with one concrete variable

You are building a corporate default prediction model, and among the inputs is the number of times the loan has been restructured. The variable looks entirely reasonable - firms in difficulty restructure often. The problem is that most restructurings are recorded AFTER the firm has already run into serious trouble, sometimes even after the point at which it is marked as in default. So the model is reading the answer. The test results are implausibly good, and they collapse on the first day of live running, because at prediction time that variable does not exist yet.

sections.label: A random split is itself a form of leakage
sections.text: With financial data, a random 80/20 split puts June's observations in the training set and March's in the test set - which is to say the model learns from the future in order to predict the past. It does not reproduce the real situation, where you only have data up to today. The right split is by time: train on the earlier period, test on the later one, and ideally leave a gap between the two so that lagged variables cannot bridge the boundary.

left.label: A model with economic theory behind it
left.text: When the market changes it degrades gradually and in a predictable direction, because the relationships it leans on have a reason to exist. You usually notice it weakening before it does damage.

right.label: A purely data-driven model
right.text: It can break abruptly, because the relationship it found may be a feature of the training period rather than a mechanism. That is why it needs TIGHTER monitoring, not looser - ordinary intuition runs the other way.
